title: Device architecture and trust boundaries
basic: A sensor measures the world; an actuator changes it. Firmware manages hardware, while gateways, brokers, cloud APIs and apps move or consume data.
intermediate: Draw each identity and trust boundary separately. A gateway forwarding a reading does not establish that the reading is genuine.
advanced: Model compromise of one device, one tenant and the update service separately. Keep physical safety constraints independent of cloud availability.
example: A fictional greenhouse sensor may publish temperature, but must never authorize an irrigation command.

title: Inventory and a safe assessment plan
basic: Record the device model, firmware version, owner, interfaces and expected behavior before testing.
intermediate: Use a spare isolated device or simulator, synthetic data, a recovery image and a maintenance window. Capture baseline behavior first.
advanced: Include dependent cloud services, radios and recovery procedures in scope. Stop if timing changes, resets or physical effects exceed agreed limits.
example: Document a maximum request rate and a stop condition; do not run intrusive scans against a working lock or medical device.

title: Threat modeling and attack surfaces
basic: Assets include readings, credentials, update keys, availability and actuator state. Entry points include radio, debug ports, APIs and update files.
intermediate: Describe attacker access: remote network, nearby radio, authenticated tenant or physical possession. These produce different risks.
advanced: Trace a proposed path across boundaries and identify evidence for every step. A version banner alone does not establish exploitability.
example: Finding an open port is an observation; prove the specific unintended permission on a lab device before assigning impact.

title: Identity, provisioning and ownership
basic: Give each device an individual identity. Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides allowed operations.
intermediate: Use controlled onboarding and rotate or revoke credentials when a device changes owner. Avoid credentials shared across an entire fleet.
advanced: Consider key storage, enrollment abuse, lost devices and recovery. A client-provided device ID is not proof of possession of its credential.
example: Test owner access and another fictional owner against the same synthetic device record.

title: MQTT brokers, topics and permissions
basic: MQTT sends publications through a broker to subscribed clients. Topic names organize data; they are not access controls.
intermediate: Review publish and subscribe permissions separately. Understand retained messages, session persistence and wildcard subscriptions before using test data.
advanced: QoS delivery semantics do not authorize commands or make an actuator operation safe to repeat. Use application-level command IDs and bounded deduplication.
example: Allow sensor-a to publish lab/sensor-a/telemetry; deny lab/sensor-b/telemetry and wildcard access. Reference: MQTT 5.0 specification.

title: CoAP and constrained services
basic: CoAP provides request/response semantics for constrained environments. The base specification commonly uses UDP.
intermediate: Inspect resources, methods and identity-to-resource permissions in a local fixture. Observe retransmissions and resource limits.
advanced: Review transport or object security in the actual deployment; DTLS and OSCORE protect different boundaries. Do not infer protection from a port number.
example: Compare an authorized resource read with a denied read of another simulated device; never assume discovery grants access.

title: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth LE, Zigbee and Thread
basic: Radio proximity creates a separate attack surface. These technologies differ in link behavior, discovery and enrollment.
intermediate: Document pairing or joining, key lifecycle, permitted peers and gateway behavior for the exact implementation. Thread carries IPv6; Matter is an application-layer ecosystem, not a radio.
advanced: Assess commissioning, ownership transfer and recovery in an isolated radio lab. Encryption does not fix weak onboarding or overbroad application permissions.
example: Make a comparison worksheet: link technology, enrollment step, identity, key storage, revocation and application authorization.

title: UART, JTAG and physical interfaces
basic: UART is a serial interface; JTAG supports hardware test and debugging. Exposed pads do not automatically mean an accessible privileged console.
intermediate: Use the manufacturer pinout and voltage requirements on a spare powered-down board before attaching suitable equipment. Incorrect voltage can damage hardware.
advanced: Review production debug policy and physical attack assumptions. A disabled software console and hardware debug lockdown are separate controls.
example: Photograph and label known interfaces, record uncertainty and review documentation; do not guess pin voltage or short pads.

title: Firmware inspection and software inventory
basic: Firmware is software packaged for a device. Start with a legitimately obtained image and record its origin, version and digest.
intermediate: Inspect file types, embedded configuration and component versions offline. Do not execute unknown extracted programs. Treat apparent credentials as sensitive evidence.
advanced: Map components to actual vendor builds and configuration. A string resembling a version or password requires validation; bundled unused code may change exposure.
example: Use file and sha256sum on a copied lab image; compare hashes to track copies, without treating the digest as proof of publisher identity.

title: Secure boot and runtime trust
basic: Secure boot checks authorized software during the boot chain. It differs from encrypting storage or verifying a downloaded file.
intermediate: Identify the root of trust, what each stage verifies and how trust keys are updated. Document recovery paths.
advanced: Consider debug access, mutable configuration and compromised runtime code after boot. Verified startup alone cannot prevent every runtime vulnerability.
example: Draw boot ROM to bootloader to operating system; mark where signature verification and failure handling occur.

title: Signed updates, rollback and recovery
basic: An update needs authenticity and integrity, compatibility checks and a safe installation process.
intermediate: Verify signed metadata against a trusted key and bind it to the intended payload and device model. Plan interrupted-power recovery.
advanced: Protect against unauthorized downgrade while preserving an authenticated recovery path. Key rotation, revocation and long offline periods need explicit design.
example: A matching SHA-256 digest detects a change only relative to a trusted expected digest; a downloaded checksum beside malware proves no publisher identity.

title: Input validation, freshness and replay
basic: Treat readings and commands as untrusted structured input. Validate required fields, types and acceptable limits.
intermediate: Bind telemetry to the authenticated device and reject unexpected fields. Track sequence numbers or another freshness mechanism per identity.
advanced: Design resets, clock drift, storage persistence and concurrent delivery explicitly. A sequence counter alone is not authentication and may fail after state loss.
example: The offline exercise rejects booleans as temperatures and denies repeated sequence numbers; its replay memory disappears when restarted.

title: Mobile apps, cloud APIs and tenant isolation
basic: A device ecosystem includes APIs, dashboards and mobile apps. Apply ordinary web security principles at each service boundary.
intermediate: Test object-level authorization with two synthetic users and separate devices. Review tokens, enrollment endpoints and ownership transfer.
advanced: A secure radio link does not prevent an insecure cloud API from exposing device data. Check authorization on subscriptions, exports and administrative functions too.
example: Change only the synthetic device identifier and verify denial for the other owner, including error and cached response paths.

title: Segmentation, monitoring and retirement
basic: Separate device, management and ordinary user traffic according to required communication paths.
intermediate: Build an allowlist of necessary services and record authentication failures, update results and unexpected reconnects without logging secrets.
advanced: Plan certificate expiry, vendor end-of-support, data deletion and revocation at retirement. A factory reset may not revoke a cloud credential.
example: Write an expected-flow table and a retirement checklist, then compare actual evidence from your isolated lab.

title: Choose tools by the question
basic: Use Wireshark for captured traffic, file and sha256sum for image identification, and a text editor for configuration review.
intermediate: Binwalk can help identify embedded formats; Ghidra can support offline code understanding. Broker clients and CoAP clients exercise configured local services.
advanced: Record tool versions and exact input. Extractors process untrusted files and should run in an isolated workspace; signatures and heuristics can be wrong.
example: Explain the question first: packet contents, image structure or authorization decision. Use the smallest tool and fixture that can answer it.

title: Evidence, remediation and retesting
basic: Write the expected rule, observed result, affected model/version and prerequisites. Separate observation from confirmed impact.
intermediate: Save minimal redacted evidence and include a negative control. Suggest a specific permission, lifecycle or validation repair.
advanced: Retest the original case and a legitimate operation after repair. State coverage limits across firmware variants, radios and cloud regions.
example: Use the supplied offline policy lab, record allowed and denied outcomes, and explain why these tests do not certify real hardware.
